editorial.headline: Tropical Fruit Farming, From Field Preparation to Post-Harvest
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 01220 covers the full cultivation cycle for tropical and subtropical fruit, nationally open to PMA and available across all business scales, including in Bali.
editorial.body:
KBLI 01220 is the business classification for farming tropical and subtropical fruit. Its scope is broad, but not vague: it covers the agricultural work behind crops such as avocado, banana and plantain, dates, figs, papaya, pineapple, rambutan, durian, duku, guava, water apple, longan, jackfruit, mango, mangosteen, sapodilla, starfruit, salak, soursop, dragon fruit, and similar produce. The classification is not only about the moment of harvest. It follows the activity as a chain, beginning with land preparation and planting, continuing through crop maintenance, and ending with harvesting and post-harvest work when those steps are carried out as one integrated activity.

The record also brings seed-related activity into view. Planting tropical and subtropical fruit crops to produce seed in the form of kernels or seeds sits inside this classification, as do nursery and seed-production activities for tropical and subtropical fruit plants, including the stated example of date seed production. In practical terms, this is a cultivation code for operators whose core activity is growing the fruit or preparing the plant material that supports that cultivation. It is not framed as a trading, processing, or hospitality activity; its centre of gravity is agricultural production and the connected cultivation cycle.

The scale position is unusually clear. The code is open to Micro, Small, Medium, and Large businesses, so it can fit both a modest farm operation and a larger structured agricultural business, provided the registered activity remains within this defined scope. For a founder, that matters because the classification is not reserved only for one size of operator. The same code can describe a small fruit-growing venture, a medium farming business, or a larger agricultural company working through land preparation, planting, maintenance, harvest, and post-harvest as a continuous production activity.

On foreign ownership, the national picture is straightforward: the PMA status is open, with a maximum foreign ownership ceiling of 100%. That means the record does not impose a foreign-shareholding cap below full ownership. Bali is also not blocked on the facts given here. The Bali status is marked OK_or_HIGHER_RISK, and the reason is specific: OSS risk at Large scale is Medium-High or High, so it is not blocked by the Bali moratorium. The moratorium itself blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA across Bali, but this record does not place KBLI 01220 inside that blocked outcome. The honest reading is therefore clean: nationally, this activity is foreign-open up to 100%, and in Bali it is not blocked by the moratorium on the record supplied.
